title.home: Preflight: fly the whole run before you pay for it
nav.label: Preflight
home.eyebrow: A flight simulator for ML jobs
home.lede: Preflight runs a few minutes of your real training job, learns how it behaves, and lets you move any setting and watch memory, time and cost answer at once. GPU time is spent only to check the plan you pick.
home.scroll: Scroll to see how it works
home.probe.title: Probe
home.probe.body: Minutes of real steps on a real GPU. A live flight's numbers start from a measurement; each sample says whether its numbers are illustrative or measured.
home.simulate.title: Simulate
home.simulate.body: Move a knob and the map, memory and cost answer in under 400 ms, computed in your browser.
home.verify.title: Verify
home.verify.body: When the plan looks right, one short real run confirms it before the long one starts.
home.closing: Catch the crash at the first eval before it costs you a night.

newflight.private.label: Private triage
newflight.private.body: For this check-in's probes, Muse Glimmer reads each log on Preflight's own GPU instead of Muse Spark Open on Baseten, so those logs reach our Modal container, not Meta or Baseten. Probes you run later from the record are read by Muse Spark Open as usual.
newflight.private.map: Muse Spark (Meta) still reads your code to build the map.
newflight.private.diagnosis: Muse Spark's check of the record's plots against its numbers is skipped for this check-in.
newflight.private.wait: Muse Glimmer stops when nobody has used it for a while, so the first triage after that can take several minutes while it starts (about 5 to 8 minutes on 1 Nov). Once it is running, a triage takes seconds.

detail.label: Details for {name}
detail.about.data: Loading and tokenising runs on the CPU, so a faster GPU makes it a bigger share of the step, not a smaller one.
detail.about.forward: The model's blocks are drawn once with how many times they repeat. Activations from here are held until backward.
detail.about.loss: Cross-entropy over the vocabulary. Logits for long examples are a hidden memory cost.
detail.about.backward: Gradients flow back through every block. With checkpointing on, forward work is redone here and memory drops.
detail.about.optimizer: The optimiser keeps extra numbers for every trainable weight. With LoRA that is the adapters only.
detail.about.eval: Evaluation runs every few hundred steps at its own batch size. If it keeps activations, it can need more memory than training.
detail.about.checkpoint: Each save writes the trainable state to disk. On a preemptible queue, the gap between saves is the work you can lose.

guide.label: Guide
guide.intro: I'll walk you through the few knobs that matter most for this job, aiming for {aim}, and move each one on the map so you can see what it does.
guide.needs_code: This needs a code change. Muse Code writes it in a sandbox and a short verify run checks it.
guide.fallback: The live guide isn't available right now, so the rule-based tour is running instead.
guide.cliff: {knob} at {value} crosses the memory limit: peak {peak} of {cap}.
guide.cliff_no_peak: {knob} at {value} runs out of memory on this GPU ({cap}).
guide.done: That's the tour. No other single move improves your aim.
guide.done.why: The tour stops when no knob it may move improves the aim without risking a failure, or when every useful knob is pinned or already toured.
guide.nothing_safe: Something on the map is likely to fail, and no knob the model can answer for fixes it yet. Measuring the fix is the honest next step.
guide.nothing_safe.tight: This could run out of memory, and no knob the model can answer for lowers that chance yet. Measuring is the honest next step.
guide.nothing_safe.none.why: Nothing this record's predictions cover lowers it, so there's no setting to measure yet; the findings on the map are where to look.
guide.nothing_safe.why: The fix sits outside what this record's predictions cover, so the guide won't guess. A probe at the fixed setting measures it; it costs a little GPU time and waits for your go-ahead.
guide.pin_blocks_fix: {knob} is pinned, and moving it to {to} is what would make the run fit.
guide.pin_blocks_saving: {knob} is pinned. Releasing it to {to} would change {target} by {delta}.
guide.pin_blocks.why: The guide never moves a pinned knob. When the aim can't be met with your pins, it names the pin in the way and what releasing it would buy.
guide.ask.label: What are you doing, and what matters most?
guide.ask.placeholder: Fine-tune a 7B model on our support tickets, one A100, done by Friday, cheapest possible.
guide.approval.run_probe: The guide wants to measure this on a real GPU. Measuring costs a little money, so it waits for you.
guide.approval.propose_patch: The guide wants Muse Code to write this code change. That costs a little money, so it waits for you.
guide.approval.run_verify: The guide wants one real run of this plan to verify it. That costs a little money, so it waits for you.
guide.approval.unavailable: Live measuring opens with the probe queue
guide.rule.eval_batch_size.fix.line: Your eval pass is the risk. At eval batch {from} it needs more memory than this GPU has, so the run would stop at the first eval. Eval batch {to} peaks at {peak} of {cap}, and changes {target} by {delta}.
guide.rule.eval_batch_size.fix.why: Eval runs every few hundred steps at its own batch size. Here it keeps activations as if it were training, so at a large eval batch it holds more than the whole training step.
guide.rule.eval_batch_size.save.line: An eval batch of {to} changes {target} by {delta}.
guide.rule.eval_batch_size.save.why: Larger eval batches finish evaluation sooner, as long as they still fit beside the training state.
guide.rule.batch_size.fix.line: A batch of {to} instead of {from} fits in memory, and changes {target} by {delta}.
guide.rule.batch_size.fix.why: Activations grow with batch size times sequence length, so a smaller batch shrinks them.
guide.rule.batch_size.save.line: A batch of {to} keeps the GPU busier: {target} changes by {delta}.
guide.rule.batch_size.save.why: Small batches leave the GPU waiting between kernels. A larger batch does more work per launch, until memory runs out.
guide.rule.seq_len.fix.line: Sequences of {to} tokens instead of {from} fit in memory. That changes what the model sees, so check it suits your data.
guide.rule.seq_len.fix.why: Activations and logits grow with sequence length. Shorter sequences fit, but long examples get cut.
guide.rule.gradient_checkpointing.fix.li: Checkpointing frees activation memory so the run fits. Steps get slower: {target} changes by {delta}.
guide.rule.gradient_checkpointing.fix.wh: Checkpointing keeps only each block's input and recomputes the rest during backward, trading compute for memory.
guide.rule.gradient_checkpointing.save.w: Checkpointing saves memory at the cost of recomputation. It pays off when the freed memory lets a cheaper GPU or a bigger batch work.
guide.rule.gpu.fix.line: On {to}, the run fits in memory, and {target} changes by {delta}.
guide.rule.gpu.fix.why: A GPU with more memory removes the limit without touching the code.
guide.rule.gpu.save.line: Is a different GPU worth it? On {to}, {target} changes by {delta}.
guide.rule.gpu.save.why: A pricier GPU can be cheaper overall when it finishes fast enough. Predictions for a GPU that wasn't probed are extrapolated from its specs, so verify before you commit.
guide.rule.generic.fix.line: Moving {knob} from {from} to {to} makes the run fit, and changes {target} by {delta}.
guide.rule.generic.fix.why: Of the moves that clear the predicted failure, this one costs your aim the least.
guide.rule.generic.save.why: This is the knob whose best single move improves your aim the most without risking a failure.
guide.combo.line: None of the single changes left clears the out-of-memory risk here. Together, {changes} bring peak memory to {combo_peak}, with a {combo_risk} chance of running out.
guide.combo.line_nopeak: None of the single changes left clears the out-of-memory risk here. Together, {changes} leave a {combo_risk} chance of running out.
guide.combo.line_tight: None of the single changes left clears the out-of-memory risk here. Together, {changes} come close: peak memory {combo_peak}, with a {combo_risk} chance of running out, so it's worth measuring before you rely on it.
guide.combo.line_nopeak_tight: None of the single changes left clears the out-of-memory risk here. Together, {changes} come close, with a {combo_risk} chance of running out, so it's worth measuring before you rely on it.
guide.combo.measure_ask: Please measure this combination before I apply it: {changes} ({ids}).
guide.combo.why: {first} alone isn't enough at this setting. The record's predictions cover these changes together, so this is one prediction for the combination, not a sum of separate guesses.
guide.combo.why_plain: The record's predictions cover these changes together, so this is one prediction for the combination, not a sum of separate guesses.
guide.combo.why_rows: {first} alone isn't enough at this setting. {rows_cut} The record's predictions cover these changes together, so this is one prediction for the combination, not a sum of separate guesses.
guide.combo.why_plain_rows: {rows_cut} The record's predictions cover these changes together, so this is one prediction for the combination, not a sum of separate guesses.
guide.combo.rows.none: A sequence length of {to} cuts no row short: the longest is {max} tokens.
guide.combo.rows.few: A sequence length of {to} cuts at most 1 row in 1,000 short: the 99.9th percentile row is {p999} tokens.
guide.combo.rows.few_n: A sequence length of {to} cuts at most 1 row in 1,000 short (no more than {most} of {rows}): the 99.9th percentile row is {p999} tokens.
guide.combo.rows.some: A sequence length of {to} cuts short every row longer than that. Half the rows are at most {p50} tokens, and no more than 1 in 1,000 is longer than {p999}.
guide.combo.rows.most: A sequence length of {to} cuts at least half the rows short: the median row is {p50} tokens.
guide.combo.label: A combined move
guide.rule.aim_unpredicted.line: Your aim isn't predicted for this run yet, but its memory is measured: moving {knob} from {from} to {to} changes {target} by {delta}.
guide.rule.aim_unpredicted.why: The number your aim needs isn't predicted at this setting, so the guide won't rank moves by it; it ranks the ones it can answer for, on memory, which the probes measured.

fitmap.title: Fit
fitmap.help: Each square is this run at one pair of settings, with every other knob as it is on the dials. Its fill is the predicted peak memory as a share of the GPU's; its colour and mark are the chance of running out of memory: under {fits} fits, {fits} to {fails} is tight, over {fails} fails, and hatched means the prediction isn't trusted there. The solid edge is where fits ends and the dashed one where fails begins, placed from memory predicted between the squares. Move any knob, or the GPU, and the map redraws. Point at a square to preview it, press it to fly there, or drag your run's square.

measured.title: Measured
checks.title: Held-out checks on real runs
checks.method: Every probe in a real run is held out in turn: the engine predicts that probe's setting from the rest of the record, and the prediction is scored against what the probe measured. Probes of the same point are held out together, so each prediction has one probe fewer than the cockpit has. Memory is compared on reserved bytes; for a probe that ran no eval pass, the engine's eval share comes off its prediction. Abstentions are listed, not scored. Step time, memory and the interval get a status only when the whole Wilson 95% interval is past their bar; one missed out-of-memory is a miss whatever the count. Checks from one run share its script and GPU, so they aren't independent, though the intervals treat them as if they were.

onboard.map.title: Your job, as a map
onboard.map.body: Each part of the run is drawn on the loop, sized by its share of a step. Click one for its numbers and anything Preflight found there.
onboard.readouts.title: The readouts
onboard.readouts.body: The run's headline numbers, such as how long it takes, what it costs and how likely it is to fail, each with the range Preflight expects. A hatched readout is one Preflight won't vouch for at this setting.
onboard.knobs.title: The knobs
onboard.knobs.body: Your job's settings. Move one and the map and readouts follow. Pin a knob to keep it where it is.
onboard.guide.title: The guide
onboard.guide.body: Not sure where to start? The guide walks you through the knobs that matter most for your aim, one move at a time, and you decide whether to keep each.

guide.campaign.grid: This plan prices a whole research grid: {runs} runs, shared across {lanes} lanes ({people}). The runs that go ahead cost {usd}, likely between {lo} and {hi}.
guide.campaign.grid.why: Each run's time and cost come from this record's predictions with their 90% ranges. The planner adds what a shared cluster does on top: splitting runs at the job time limit, interruptions and resubmits. It never adds accuracy the predictions don't have.
guide.campaign.cut: {cut} of the {runs} runs don't fit. At the table's rates, which the plan was made at, the whole grid could cost up to {grid_hi}, over the {budget} budget, so the dearest runs are cut; they're listed under Not scheduled. The runs left cost at most {cut_hi} there, at the top of their range.
guide.campaign.cut.why: The planner assumes the runs err together (the same script and the same model), so the grid's range is as wide as it can honestly be, and it cuts against the high end of that range rather than the middle.
guide.campaign.finish: The last run most likely ends {p50} UTC; in 80% of the simulated campaigns it ends between {p10} and {p90}. That's the band under the lanes.
guide.campaign.finish.why: A finish date isn't one number: the planner runs the campaign thousands of times, each run's time drawn from its range and interruptions at the cluster's rate, and reports when the last run ends.
guide.campaign.finish_abstain: The planner doesn't give a finish date for this grid: {finish_why}.

rl.spread.why: When every answer to a prompt scores the same, GRPO's advantage is zero for all of them, so that prompt doesn't move the model.

guide.rl.spread: {k} of {n} prompts gave GRPO nothing to learn from: every answer to each of them scored the same ({share}; 95% interval {lo} to {hi}, measured). {never} of them got no correct answer at all.
guide.rl.spread.why: GRPO learns from the difference between answers to the same prompt. At group size {g} the engine predicts {pred} of groups with no spread. A bigger group helps prompts that sometimes pass; prompts that never pass need easier prompts or a model that already solves some of them.
guide.rl.length: The longest completion reached the {cap}-token cap, and 5% ran past {p95} tokens. {trunc_line}
guide.rl.length_under: The longest completion was {longest} tokens, under the {cap}-token cap; 5% ran past {p95}. {trunc_line}
guide.rl.length.why: A completion cut at the cap is scored as it stands, often without its final answer, so a cap that's too tight can turn long, correct reasoning into a zero reward.
guide.rl.trunc_estimated: Truncation wasn't measured on this run; from the length distribution it's about {trunc}.
